    Method concordance

    Source: vignettes/method-concordance.Rmd
    method-concordance.Rmd

    The official supplementary methods for Torres-García et al. (2022) were reviewed against engine mssr_r_rev3 on 24 October 2026 and re-checked against the article, the supplement and the pinned R and Python scripts on 27 October 2026. This comparison documents the defined single-frame operator and its differences from the authors’ code. The MATLAB code and the Fiji plugin were not compared.

    Sources:

    • Original article, DOI 10.1038/s41467-022-34693-9.
    • Official supplementary information, 69 pages; SHA-256 a48d05079a4f32fa7fe1748f6937f27308a43ba0e452aabb9841229bc85583e2.
    • Author implementation revision 77b20b1, including the R and Python scripts and user manual.

    Single-frame correspondence

    Operation Published location Rev3 correspondence and boundary
    Neighbourhood S17, p.8; Fig. S8, p.18 The default punctured disk follows the spatial support. Radius is max(1, round(amp*fwhm/2)), using half-even rounding by default. The named square option follows the Python backend’s different support.
    Local weights and mean shift S25–S29, pp.9–10; S48, p.17 Adaptive range-normalized Gaussian weights; centre minus weighted neighbour mean, with negatives clipped. Rev3 evaluates the equivalent weighted sum of local differences to reduce cancellation.
    Cubic interpolation S50–S51, p.26 Published c=1/2 is exactly the separable Keys kernel a=-1/2, and S50 is the separable product that rev3 implements. Grid alignment and repeated half-sample reflection are package conventions; the authors’ backends differ (below).
    Mesh compensation Note 6.1.2, pp.27–28 Average of the image and four symmetric axial shifts. Rev3 specifies ceil(amp/2) and reflected edges, correcting the upstream R shift asymmetry.
    Refinement Note 5.1.2/Fig. S11, p.21; article Fig. 2a Subtraction, complement, normalization and current-map multiplication agree for finite nondegenerate steps; each further order starts from the previous map, as the article’s Fig. 2a legend and both scripts describe. Frame-wide maxima make independently normalized tiles different from a whole-frame computation.
    Output weighting Note 11.4, p.60 Optional multiplication of the normalized structure map by the amplified input. Rev3 preserves orientation, correcting the R script’s rotation/multiplication mismatch. Weighted values remain nonquantitative.

    S51 cites Keys’s cubic convolution and a two-dimensional cubic convolution (Reichenbach and Geng 2003); the latter develops a nonseparable kernel, but S50 is the separable product. The authors’ scripts interpolate with neither: the R script calls akima’s bicubic.grid (revised Akima method), and the Python script calls SciPy’s interp2d, so its default bicubic path (ftI = False) fails on SciPy 1.14 and later. Both sample endpoint-aligned positions, which grid = "endpoint" reproduces; the default grid = "extent" preserves the field of view. With the R script’s asymmetric mesh shifts as well, the amplified input already differs beyond rounding, and MSSR’s range normalization and refinement are nonlinear and can enlarge such differences locally. Pixel-wise agreement with the authors’ amplified maps is therefore not expected.

    Supplementary Note 6 and the Python script also offer Fourier interpolation, which the article uses for temporal analysis; mssrscopR does not implement it. The paper also describes scaling zero-order output to the original maximum (p.17), which differs from optional pixelwise weighting. Rev3 fixes its two output roles explicitly. Flat-input results, zero-range handling, skipped undefined refinement, arithmetic conditioning and resource refusals are documented implementation extensions. Quota masks are a separate package feature.

    Numerical and scientific limits

    The source review does not expand numerical qualification: 76 cases at orders 0–3 pass within the sampled synthetic domain; two of the wider 98 cases fail at order 10. Orders above 3 retain an explicit warning. Passing cases do not prove accuracy for every input, parameter combination or derived mask.

    The Gaussian theorem’s displayed derivative in S33 omits weight-derivative terms despite the weights’ intensity dependence. This review does not supply a proof for the full adaptive operator or assert that the theorem’s conclusion is false. Physical calibration, measured PSFs, resolution gain and application benefit remain separate requirements.

    Temporal and dimensional restrictions

    Temporal functions remain unsupported. Table S2 (p.25) and the pinned scripts contain material differences:

    • TPM has an unspecified j index in the table; both scripts compute the square of the frame sum.
    • The table uses population variance; the R script uses sample variance and a different missing-data policy. The table labels Var/Mean as CV.
    • The displayed SOFI formulas use signed, distinct-lag products. The Python implementation instead uses absolute deviations, and its shifted slices are re-aligned so that all factors come from one frame: orders 2 and 3 average |δx_k|² and |δx_k|³, and order 4 returns |⟨|δx|⁴⟩ − 3⟨|δx|²⟩²|.

    Any future temporal operator needs a resolved formula and independent qualification on genuine repeated-time data. Wavelength, depth and lifetime-delay axes cannot be substituted for time. Note 10.7 (p.54) explicitly leaves a full anisotropic 3D extension for further development.

    The article’s open-access licence and the user guide’s plugin-specific public-domain statement do not resolve every upstream script or dependency’s redistribution terms. No upstream implementation or source payload is included in this qualification kit.
